---
title: Training options
description: "Logging, validation cadence, loops, batch size, optimization, and local distributed training."
---

[Train and save](../learn/train-and-save.qmd) covers the first run: one
`model.fit(...)` call that binds the data, selects hardware, stops early, and
restores the best checkpoint. This guide expands on that call: logging and
validation cadence, loops, batch size, optimization, and
local distributed training. Saving, parameter averaging, and resuming have
their own page, [Checkpoints, EMA, and resuming](checkpoints-ema-and-resuming.qmd).

## Fit a model

Continue with the [transaction-history model](../learn/add-transaction-history.qmd)
and independent, application-supplied Parquet files at `payments/history/train.parquet`
and `payments/history/validation.parquet`. Each row keeps the latest payment and its
predecessors together in `trxns`. Every transaction has a supervised
`disputed` label, kept out of the input by `mask=True`.

```python
import relflow as rf

datamodule = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/history/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/history/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(
    datamodule,
    batch_size=128,
    learning_rate=1e-4,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    max_epochs=30,
    checkpoint_dir="checkpoints/payments",
)
```

For eager Polars frames, use `rf.PolarsDataModule`. It converts the frames to Arrow
at ingress. See [Data modules](data-modules.qmd) for source and split choices.
Each loop binds an unbound data module to its model before loading. See
[automatic binding](data-modules.qmd#bind-a-model-when-the-loop-starts) for ownership
and native Lightning behavior.

Early stopping and rollback are enabled by default. Both monitor `loss/validate`
in `min` mode; patience is ten validation checks and `min_delta` is zero. Full
best and last checkpoints are saved. Without `checkpoint_dir`, the run uses a
unique directory under `default_root_dir/checkpoints`. Fitting restores the best
model state, including schema, vocabularies, and normalizers, before returning
the model. Read [Evaluation](../learn/evaluation.qmd) before choosing a monitor.

## Report progress and validate

`Model.track` uses Lightning's native logging: training metrics are logged only
per step. `log_every_n_steps`, defaulting to 50, controls
how often attached loggers receive step metrics. Step values describe the latest
batch, rather than an average over that interval. With gradient accumulation,
logging follows optimizer updates. Set `log_every_n_steps=0` to disable step
emission while retaining internal loss averages and validation/test metrics.

Training metrics keep their names, such as `loss/train` and
`.trxns.disputed/train.loss.content`. The training loss average is available to
callbacks as `loss/train_epoch` and is not sent to attached loggers. Validation
and test retain pass aggregates; `loss/validate` remains the default checkpoint
and early-stopping monitor. `Model.track(..., on_epoch=True)` explicitly opts
into epoch logging for a custom metric. More frequent logging does not run validation, save
checkpoints, change patience, or advance schedulers. See
[Evaluation](../learn/evaluation.qmd) for metric definitions.

With a Lightning logger configured by your application as `application_logger`:

```python
model.fit(datamodule, logger=application_logger, log_every_n_steps=50)
```

For learning-rate logging, add Lightning's `LearningRateMonitor` to `callbacks`.

Validation normally runs at the end of each epoch. To evaluate long training
streams more frequently, supply an integer `val_check_interval` in **training
batches**. With `check_val_every_n_epoch=None`, the interval continues across
epoch boundaries:

```python
model.fit(
    datamodule,
    logger=application_logger,
    log_every_n_steps=50,
    val_check_interval=1_000,
    check_val_every_n_epoch=None,
)
```

Early stopping and best-checkpoint selection follow validation. Patience counts
validation checks with no improvement, so increasing validation frequency can
stop training sooner. Keep the held-out observations and masking policy
consistent across checks. Checkpoint filenames include both epoch and optimizer
step to distinguish evaluations within one epoch. Make sure a configured fit
runs long enough to reach validation when its selection policies require it.

All loops process their configured splits without automatic time or batch caps.
Use explicit batch limits for smoke tests or deliberate sampling:

```python
model.fit(datamodule, max_epochs=1, limit_train_batches=10, limit_val_batches=2)
model.validate(datamodule, limit_val_batches=100)
model.test(datamodule, limit_test_batches=100)
```

Use integer batch counts for Arrow iterable loaders. Data-module sampling and
`epoch_size` remain explicit data-selection choices. Lightning's `max_time` sets
a budget for the whole fit. `fast_dev_run=True` skips automatic early stopping
and rollback for Lightning's single-pass diagnostic run.

## Choose the loop

| Call | Required data split | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model.fit(datamodule)` | `train` and, for the default policies, `validate` | Optimize and restore the best model. |
| `model.validate(datamodule)` | `validate` | Return one metric dictionary per loader. |
| `model.test(datamodule)` | `test` | Return held-out metrics per loader. |
| `model.predict(datamodule=...)` | `predict` | Collect an Arrow table on one device or stream with a Writer. |

Stages also control masking and field-owned learning, such as vocabulary and
normalizer updates. Use the corresponding split rather than repurposing a
training loader for inference. For bounded requests, the separate
`model.predict(observations)` convenience returns an Arrow table without a
Trainer; see [Prediction output](../reference/prediction-output.qmd).

Hardware defaults to `accelerator="auto"`, `devices="auto"`,
`strategy="ddp_find_unused_parameters_true"` for multiple devices or nodes,
and BF16 mixed precision when all selected devices support it. Otherwise
precision is FP32. Unused-parameter detection supports parameters omitted from
a batch's reconstruction objectives. Supply explicit `accelerator`, `devices`,
`precision`, or `strategy` to override these choices. Other Trainer arguments
pass through; `callbacks` works on all four loops. relflow installs its
required callbacks automatically.
Compile
selected model regions before the loop with `model.compile()` if desired;
[Performance](performance.qmd) describes exactly what this compiles.

## Batch size

Set `batch_size` on `fit`, `validate`, `test`, or `predict`. It must be a positive
integer. The value updates `model.batch_size` and remains current for later
loops; omitting it or passing `None` leaves that setting unchanged.

```python
model.fit(datamodule, batch_size=128, max_epochs=30)
model.validate(validation_data, batch_size=256)
model.test(test_data, batch_size=256)
model.predict(datamodule=prediction_data, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

Here `validation_data`, `test_data`, and `prediction_data` are application data
modules supplying their corresponding named splits. `ArrowDataModule` reads
the model's current batch size when creating each loader. Custom Lightning data
modules own their loader configuration; changing the model setting does not
reconfigure a custom prebuilt loader.

Under DDP the size is per device. With two devices and `batch_size=128`, a
complete distributed training batch contains 256 observations before gradient
accumulation. The constructor's `batch_size` remains the initial setting,
defaulting to one, and is saved in the model artifact. Native Trainer and Tuner
workflows can continue to use it.

For direct in-memory Arrow input, setting `batch_size=256` on `model.predict(...)` also
chunks the processed observations before encoding. Omitting that override
preserves whole-input execution. See
[Direct prediction batches](../reference/prediction-output.qmd#batch-direct-requests).

## Configure optimization and callbacks

Configure AdamW on `fit(...)`. Omitted options use these effective defaults:

| Option | Default | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `learning_rate` | `1e-3` | AdamW learning rate. |
| `weight_decay` | `0.01` | Decay for eligible parameters. |
| `betas` | `(0.9, 0.95)` | First- and second-moment coefficients. |
| `eps` | `1e-8` | Numerical stability term. |
| `fused` | `True` | Fused Torch AdamW; `False` disables it and `None` delegates to Torch. |
| `decay_bias` | `False` | Allow decay on bias parameters. |
| `decay_1d` | `False` | Allow decay on scalar and one-dimensional parameters. |
| `no_decay_name_fragments` | `("norm",)` | Case-insensitive parameter-name fragments excluded from decay. |

Built-in AdamW binds the current parameters when training starts. Every ordinary
fit creates fresh optimizer state, including after schema mutation or rollback.
Options supplied to one call do not become defaults for the next call:

```python
model.fit(datamodule, learning_rate=1e-3, max_epochs=30)
model.fit(datamodule, learning_rate=1e-4, weight_decay=0.01, max_epochs=30)
```

The second run starts from the first run's restored best model, with new
optimization state. Use [`ckpt_path`](checkpoints-ema-and-resuming.qmd#resume-training) to continue a saved
run's optimizer, scheduler, and loop progress instead.

Pass any scheduler as `fit(scheduler=...)` for that run. A scheduler factory
receives `(model, optimizer)` and returns a scheduler or Lightning scheduler
configuration. Prefer a factory so it binds the optimizer created for the
current call; a scheduler bound to another optimizer is rejected. A scheduler
supplied to a previous fit is not reused automatically.

For custom optimization, `fit(optimizer=...)` accepts an optimizer instance or
a factory receiving the model. Factories should collect the current parameters;
reusing an optimizer built before mutation or rollback can refer to replaced
modules and is rejected. Custom optimizer instances manage their own state.
An explicit optimizer cannot be combined with the built-in AdamW options.
Advanced `Model(optimizer=..., scheduler=...)` or model-attribute configurations
remain defaults for native Lightning workflows and custom fits; ordinary fits
need no separate optimizer assignment.

Set `early_stopping=False` or `rollback=False` to disable either policy. Train-only
fitting disables both or explicitly chooses a training monitor such as
`loss/train_epoch`. Each policy also accepts a configured `rf.EarlyStopping` or
`rf.RollbackCheckpoint` callback. Policy callbacks in `callbacks` replace their
automatic defaults; other Lightning callbacks run alongside the built-ins.

Direct `lit.Trainer.fit(...)` requires an explicit optimizer configuration,
such as `model.optimizer = rf.adamw(learning_rate=1e-3)`. Use Trainer directly
when a Lightning tool needs it; the model methods accept its execution options
for ordinary loops.

## Local distributed training

For CPU distributed training on one Mac, if Gloo aborts with
`uv_accept: invalid argument`, select the loopback interface before launching
your training script:

```bash
GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=lo0 uv run python train.py
```

This keeps communication between local ranks on macOS's loopback interface.
For training across machines, select a network interface reachable from every
rank. PyTorch documents this setting under
[Gloo network interface configuration](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#choosing-the-network-interface-to-use).

To learn from unlabeled transaction records before the supervised task, see
[Pretraining and fine-tuning](../learn/pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd). That is an optional separate workflow.
If a run fails, [Troubleshooting](../reference/troubleshooting.qmd) lists the first checks
for binding, optimizer, checkpoint, and EMA errors.
